newsitem.title: GERMANY: TIETMEYER - STABILITY PACT NEEDED TO SECURE EMU.
newsitem.headline: TIETMEYER - STABILITY PACT NEEDED TO SECURE EMU.

text.p: Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said on Thursday that a stability pact was necessary to stop the European monetary union from ripping apart.
Speaking to journalists in Bonn, Tietmeyer added that this stability pact should be as close as possible to that envisioned by German finance minister Theo Waigel.
"We are in favour of a hard currency union and against a weak currency union. Fiscal discipline must be secured, or else the danger that the EMU could be torn apart is very high," said Tietmeyer.

Asked what he meant with past calls for a "strict and narrow" interpretation of the criteria for entry to monetary union laid down in the Maastricht Treaty, Tietmeyer made clear this did not mean a fixation with specific numbers.

The Maastricht Treaty calls for countries to meet targets in inflation and exchange rates, interest rates and budget levels. But the budget clauses leave some leeway to allow for unusual conditions which may present a country with special problems in achieving the precise goals.
Responding to the question, Tietmeyer replied that the clause had to be read and applied in full, allowing for appropriate application of the additional clauses.
"Strict and narrow means the strict and narrow application of both the figures themselves and the additional comments which go alongside," he said.

Making clear that agreement on a stability pact to ensure fiscal discipline within EMU was not sufficient to allow countries to relax budget consolidation efforts, Tietmeyer said only nations that were totally ready should join EMU.

He warned that political tension on issues such as tax policies could otherwise prove divisive within monetary union, as no political union existed to back up the monetary link and provide an additional background of solidarity.
Lack of fiscal discipline could result in Europe's intergration process being marred by tremendous "political and economic conflict," he added.
